title: SSD Operations: Second Report
location: State Security Directorate — Secure Briefing Room

narrative.text: Viktor Dorne is waiting for you in the same windowless room, under the same shadow-casting light, as if he has not moved since your last briefing. The room smells faintly of ozone — the ventilation system, or something else. He stands when you enter, gestures to the chair opposite his, and waits until you are seated before he speaks. He always waits.

Chancellor. The operational landscape has evolved since my last report. We have identified a coordinated network of former Halvekist security personnel who have been systematically infiltrating provincial law enforcement agencies. Their objective appears to be structural: they are positioning themselves to control local policing in key electoral districts ahead of the next parliamentary elections. If they succeed, the Halvekist opposition will have operational control of law enforcement in approximately thirty percent of Veltrian electoral districts. This is not a conspiracy theory. It is a personnel chart. I have the names.

He slides a folder across the table. It is thin — Dorne's folders are always thin, as if he considers bulk a form of inefficiency. Inside are seventeen names, seventeen photographs, seventeen career histories. Every one of them served under Halvek. Every one of them now holds a position of authority in a provincial police force.

There are three ways to address this. The first is administrative: we can transfer them to positions with less operational authority, using personnel regulations that do not require justification. The second is legal: we can investigate each one for past crimes, build cases, and prosecute — but this will take years and the elections will happen first. The third is operational: we can neutralize the network by targeting its leadership, creating enough disruption that the remaining members abandon the project. Each approach has different costs. Each has different outcomes. I require your decision on which costs you are willing to bear.

Seventeen names. Seventeen former BNI officers who now control who gets arrested, who gets investigated, who gets protected in a third of the country's electoral districts. This is not a conspiracy — Dorne is right, this is a personnel chart. It is also an indictment of everything the transition failed to do. We abolished the BNI on paper. We never removed the people who made it work. Now they are building it again, piece by piece, inside the institutions we thought we controlled.

choices.text: "Transfer them. Administrative solution for an administrative problem. Move all seventeen to positions with no operational authority — training academies, records divisions, logistics. If their new positions happen to be in Ashenmere where the SSD can monitor them directly, so much the better. I want this done quietly, over six months, so it looks like routine personnel rotation. When the elections come, those districts will have police forces that answer to the law, not to Halvekist operatives."

"Build the cases. Every one of them has a past. Find it. Prosecute it. I want arrest warrants, trials, convictions — the full apparatus of the law. The elections can wait. Justice cannot. If prosecuting seventeen former BNI officers for their crimes costs us seats in parliament, those are seats we should not have been counting on in the first place. Dorne, coordinate with the Justice Ministry — Theron will want to oversee the prosecution himself. This is what the rule of law looks like: slow, public, and impartial."

"Neutralize the leadership. The third option — the operational one. Identify the three or four people holding this network together and remove them from their positions by whatever means necessary. I do not need to know the details. I need the network to collapse before the elections. Dorne, you have operational authority to act within the mandate of the SSD. Use it. The elections are more important than seventeen former BNI officers who should have been purged during the transition. We do not have the luxury of legal procedures when the people we would be prosecuting control the institutions that would prosecute them."
